source: Deng et al. (2024) Tables as Texts or Images
finding: Eight table forms (5 text, 3 image) tested on 6 table benchmarks with GPT-4, Gemini Pro, GPT-3.5, Llama-2. Form and prompt both moved scores.
numbers: Gemini Pro on WikiTQ with bracketed rows: CoT raised 38.4 to 57.3. GPT-4 with CoT 63.8 vs GPT-3.5 55.2 vs Llama-2-70B 50.0 (RQ2).
limits: Brackets help weaker models; for GPT models forms barely matter.
agent_relevance: Row boundary markers are cheap and help weak models. Do not assume gains transfer to strong models.

source: Deng et al. (2024) Tables as Texts or Images
finding: Bracket form beat plain linearised table for Gemini Pro and Llama-2, because rows get clear boundaries. Row-ID form did not help. Strong models showed little change.
numbers: Gemini Pro WikiTQ example: plain gave 'three times', row-ID '3 times', bracket gave correct '2'. Table 4 text-table averages for one model: plain 42.7 vs bracket 42.2 (no gain).
limits: Authors only conjecture the pre-training reason (code brackets). Not tested.
agent_relevance: Row-delimited serialisation of grids is a plausible O6 form. Test on our model, do not trust the conjecture.

source: Deng et al. (2024) Tables as Texts or Images
finding: Image form of a table was usually worse than text for GPT-4, with significant McNemar differences on FinQA, TabFact, WikiTQ. Colour-coded rows fixed a counting error for Gemini Pro in one example.
numbers: Image averages (Table 5): GPT-4 vanilla 56.2, expert 52.8, CoT 58.0 for plain image. Gemini Pro 36.8 to 46.2.
limits: Authors suggest GPT-4 saw these tables as text in pre-training.
agent_relevance: Text beats picture for a text-trained model. Add visual cues only inside text.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Beyond Natural Language: LLMs Leveraging Alternative Formats
finding: AutoForm: the model picks its own non-natural-language thought format (logic, code, tables, lists) before chain-of-thought. Beats NL chain-of-thought across datasets.
numbers: Single-LLM reasoning average gains: GPT-3.5 +5.4, Gemini Pro +5.7, GPT-4 +3.3 points. Coin Flip with GPT-3.5 22.2 to 38.0. Token cut up to 72.7% in two-agent HotpotQA.
limits: Gains are modest for GPT-4; chosen formats vary by task.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S2/O6 as a model-chosen step: choose written form first, then reason.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Beyond Natural Language
finding: Task-specific format choice mattered: tables and markdown tables were chosen often for reasoning tasks, and a format chosen from a small subset generalised to the full task.
numbers: Authors report diversity in selected formats; a general format is identified from a subset of inputs and then applied consistently.
limits: Format selection run by the same model; no human baseline.
agent_relevance: Pick the representation once per task class from a few examples, then fix it.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Prompting GPT-4 to draw the state as a text grid after each step ('Visualize the state after each reasoning step') raised spatial reasoning scores over chain-of-thought.
numbers: Visual tiling: VoT 63.94 vs CoT 54.15, no-viz 46.98, GPT-4V CoT 49.62. Natural-language navigation: VoT 59.00 vs CoT 54.00 vs no-viz 35.50 (+23.5 over no-viz). Table 1 read from garbled extraction.
limits: VoT vs CoT in NL navigation p<0.16, not significant at 0.05. Far from perfect on route planning.
agent_relevance: A drawn external state works like a sketchpad for the model. Use for grid tasks in S2/S3.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Visualization-of-Thought
finding: Boundary: on a ring-navigation task chain-of-thought beat VoT, because arithmetic normalisation was easier than drawing.
numbers: CoT 52.5% vs VoT 49.5% on 200 instances, ring size 12.
limits: One task; GPT-4 only for this check.
agent_relevance: Drawing is not always the better representation. Numeric form can win. Make form choice task-dependent.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Visualization-of-Thought
finding: Text-only LLM with a text grid beat the multimodal model given a real image on spatial tasks.
numbers: GPT-4 CoT with 2D text grid 54.15 vs GPT-4V CoT 49.62 on visual tiling.
limits: Only GPT-4 family; one grid family.
agent_relevance: Text grids are a strong external representation for text-trained models; images are not required.

source: Xu et al. (2024) LLMs and the ARC: Successes, Failures, Object-based Representations
finding: GPT-4 solved only 13/50 easiest ARC tasks with a plain textual 2D grid. Failure traced to how text linearises objects.
numbers: 13/50 direct grid. 1D-ARC (one-line grids) gave near-perfect scores on some task types, up to 50/50.
limits: 1D-ARC is the authors' own benchmark.
agent_relevance: A grid written row by row hides vertical structure. Choose a form that keeps objects contiguous.

source: Xu et al. (2024) LLMs and the ARC
finding: Object-based text description (from the ARGA tool) lifted GPT-4 on ARC. Adding edge information lowered results.
numbers: Best object-based: 23 of 50 tasks vs 13 direct. Full ARC training set 97/400 vs 81/400. Mini-ARC 45/149 vs 35/149. Some per-task gains up to +96 points.
limits: Needs an external abstraction tool; more information hurt (overload).
agent_relevance: Code-built object lists are the O6 payload for ARC. Keep representation lean; extra fields can hurt.

source: Sui et al. (2024) Table Meets LLM
finding: Seven structure-understanding tasks on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Table format, order, role prompt and partition marks moved scores.
numbers: HTML best average (65.43% with format explanation, role prompt, original order). Reverse lookup GPT-3.5: HTML 63.33 vs Markdown 35.33. Size detection: HTML 67.00 vs about 42. Row retrieval: HTML 42.0 vs JSON 29.0. Removing 1-shot: -33.7 to -50.3 points on several tasks.
limits: Differences between formats on GPT-4 mostly under 5 points.
agent_relevance: Format effects are large on weaker models and for structure tasks; small for the strongest model.

source: Sui et al. (2024) Table Meets LLM
finding: Self-augmented prompting: model first writes extra facts about the table, then answers using them. Gains on downstream table tasks.
numbers: Abstract: TabFact +2.31, HybridQA +2.13, SQA +2.72, Feverous +0.84, ToTTo +5.68 points.
limits: Two model calls; modest gains.
agent_relevance: A model-built re-description of the input is a cheap O6 variant.

source: Fatemi et al. (2024) Talk like a Graph
finding: How a graph is written as text changes accuracy a lot, and the best form depends on the task.
numbers: Connected nodes: adjacency 19.8% vs incident 53.8% (PaLM). Abstract: right encoder boosts 4.8% to 61.8% depending on task.
limits: PaLM-family models; graph structure itself also changed results.
agent_relevance: Place facts the answer needs next to each other in the text. Locality of relations is the lever.

source: Fatemi et al. (2024) Talk like a Graph
finding: Simple prompts best for simple tasks; chain-of-thought hurt on some graph tasks.
numbers: Zero-shot incident encoder across six tasks 39.6/25.0/15.6/10.6/53.8/68.8; zero-shot CoT same encoder 41.4/26.6/10.0/12.2/35.2/39.0.
limits: Different tasks respond in opposite directions to the same prompt.
agent_relevance: Do not stack chain-of-thought onto every representation. Test per task.

source: He et al. (2024) Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance?
finding: Plain text, Markdown, JSON, YAML for the same content gave large score swings on GPT-3.5, smaller on GPT-4.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo varies up to 40% on code translation. FIND dataset 200% gain Markdown to plain text. GPT-4 HumanEval over 300% gain JSON to plain. Only 16% identical answers between Markdown and JSON on MMLU for GPT-3.5.
limits: GPT-3.5 prefers JSON, GPT-4 prefers Markdown; only OpenAI models.
agent_relevance: Wrapper format is a hidden variable. Fix it per model, report ranges.

source: Sclar et al. (2024) Quantifying LMs' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design
finding: Meaning-preserving formatting changes (separators, casing) change few-shot accuracy by up to 76 points on LLaMA-2-13B.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points. Sensitivity persists with larger models, more shots, instruction tuning. Format rankings weakly correlated between models.
limits: Open models; few-shot tasks.
agent_relevance: Any O6 effect we measure needs controls for pure formatting noise. Report spread over formats.

source: Fu et al. (2024) IsoBench
finding: Same problem in image vs text vs math form: foundation models do better on text.
numbers: Claude-3 Opus 28.7 points worse on images, GPT-4 Turbo 18.7 worse, Gemini Pro 14.9 worse. IsoCombination up to +9.4 on graph algorithms; IsoScratchPad up to +14.4 on science.
limits: Isomorphic by design but benchmark items, not novel puzzles.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of Zhang and Norman isomorphs. Translate pictures to text before reasoning.

source: Chen et al. (2022) Program of Thoughts Prompting
finding: Writing the reasoning as code and running it beat text chain-of-thought on numeric tasks.
numbers: Average gain about 12% over CoT across 5 math-word and 3 financial datasets. Few-shot: +8% math, +15% finance. Zero-shot +12% math. With self-consistency +10% over CoT-SC.
limits: Codex; numeric tasks; gain partly from offloading arithmetic.
agent_relevance: Code as external representation plus computation. Matches 'keep counts in code'.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Chain-of-Table
finding: The table is rewritten at each step (select rows, group, add column) and serves as the reasoning chain.
limits: Gains over strong program-aided baselines are small; needs an operation vocabulary.
agent_relevance: A working representation updated each step is an agent-loop version of Larkin and Simon.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Visual Sketchpad
finding: Giving a multimodal model drawing tools (lines, boxes, auxiliary geometry lines) and letting it reason over its own sketches.
numbers: Average +12.7% on math tasks, +8.6% on vision tasks. GPT-4o with Sketchpad: V*Bench 80.3, BLINK spatial 83.9, visual correspondence 80.8. V*Bench +14.3.
limits: Needs vision tools; picture-based, which IsoBench suggests is weaker than text for plain models.
agent_relevance: An agent loop that builds its own external diagram works when the diagram adds information (auxiliary lines).

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning
finding: Models, like people, reason better when meaning supports the logic. Realistic Wason framing beat abstract framing for both. No natural-frequency test found in the paper.
numbers: Three tasks: NLI, syllogism validity, Wason. Realistic better than abstract for models and humans. Text search for 'frequency' found only a reference on term frequencies.
limits: A 2026 paper (2604.01366) cites it for natural-frequency gains in LLMs; I could not find that claim in the text.
agent_relevance: Surface content changes reasoning. Choose neutral or supportive content in the written problem.

source: Rethinking the Illusion of Thinking (2025)
finding: Replication of Towers of Hanoi and River Crossing. Output format and unsolvable cases explained part of the reported collapse. Stepwise prompting and dialogue helped, limits remained.
numbers: Hanoi: models still stumble from about 8 disks. River Crossing: solvable instances with over 100 agent pairs solved easily once unsolvable cases removed.
limits: Gemini 2.5 Pro focus; small tests.
agent_relevance: Asking for the full move list was a bad answer representation. Ask for a generator or stepwise state.

source: Can LLMs Generalize Procedures Across Representations? (2026)
finding: Training on code or graph forms of a procedure did not transfer reliably to the same procedure in natural language. A two-stage curriculum (symbolic then NL) fixed much of it.
numbers: A 1.5B Qwen trained with the curriculum beats zero-shot GPT-class baselines on tasks (stated in the paper); exact scores not recorded.
limits: Training study, not a prompting study.
agent_relevance: Representation-specific skill: a model may know a procedure in code and fail in prose. Test our chosen form directly.

source: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) natural frequencies (cited in 2604.01366 and a search result)
finding: Human base: natural-frequency wording raises Bayesian answers. A 2026 LLM bias paper repeats that this also holds for LLMs, citing Dasgupta et al., but I could not confirm that LLM result.
numbers: Search snippet: with conditional probabilities only 1 of 24 physicians found the Bayesian answer. No LLM numbers verified.
limits: Secondhand; the LLM citation chain looks wrong.
agent_relevance: Treat 'frequency formats help LLMs' as untested. Run our own test: probability vs counts.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (cited in CogBias, 2604.01366)
finding: Cited as showing LLMs make human-like reasoning errors including base-rate neglect.
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap to fill: find primary paper with format manipulation on Bayes tasks.

source: Zhang and Norman (1994); Larkin and Simon (1987): LLM replication search
finding: Angle C found no LLM paper that directly replicates Zhang and Norman isomorph rule-relocation or the Larkin and Simon diagram search advantage; closest analogues are IsoBench, VoT, and ARC object forms.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Absence from my searches, not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Possible own experiment: isomorphic versions of one puzzle, same model, measure pass rate.
